newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Has Ortega reached end of the line in Nicaragua?.
newsitem.headline: Has Ortega reached end of the line in Nicaragua?.

text.p: After back-to-back election defeats in 1990 and 1996, longtime Sandinista strongman Daniel Ortega has probably fought his final presidential battle, politicians and analysts said on Thursday.

"Daniel Ortega fired his final bullet with this election. His party will be looking for a new leader," Luis Sanchez Sancho, congressman for the centrist National Opposition Union (UNO), told reporters.

In his long journey from Marxist guerrilla in the 1970s to khaki-clad head of the leftist Sandinista government in the 1980s to moderate, slickly marketed presidential candidate in 1996, Ortega, 50, has come to symbolise the Sandinista Front both nationally and internationally.

He became a bogeyman of U.S. policy in Latin America in the 1980s when his Sandinista government, backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba, fought an eight-year civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels that left 25,000 people dead.

When he lost the 1990 presidential vote to Violeta Chamorro, the widow of a slain newspaper publisher who headed a centrist, anti-Sandinista coalition, many predicted the demise of the Sandinistas and Ortega. But he defied his critics by keeping control of the party and re-emerging as a serious contender in the Oct. 20, 1996 election.

Needing a new image for the vote, he wore a white shirt to symbolise peace and replaced his fiery Marxist rhetoric with a moderate, pro-free-market stance, but he still remained the glue that held together the often fractious party.

Now, with Ortega apparently headed for defeat again, trailing right-winger Arnoldo Aleman of the Liberal Alliance by 49 percent to 38 percent in the preliminary vote count, analysts foresee a conflict for control of the party.

"There is a power struggle beginning now within the party. After consecutive losses, Ortega has shown he can't lead the party back to power but there are no obvious candidates to replace him in sight," analyst and ex-Sandinista Oscar Rene Vargas told Reuters. "If Ortega doesn't agree to resign, the party will split."

Ortega and his party have kept silent but speculation is mounting over a possible replacement for Ortega, who remains highly popular with the Sandinista base. Some analysts said he could remain as secretary general of the party and cede the presidential candidacy to someone else.

Danilo Morales, a Costa Rican marketing expert who guided Ortega's 1996 election campaign, said the party needed to "change radically" if it was to win the next election, choosing a more modern, sophisticated candidate than Ortega.

"I think Daniel (Ortega) should not be the next candidate, nor any members of the Sandinista old guard," Morales said in the Nicaraguan newsmagazine Confidencial. "The ideal candidate in the future should be more cosmopolitan, more intellectual, more open ... and very sensitive to social demands -- a Nicaraguan Bill Clinton."

Sanchez and Rene Vargas said they saw no strong candidates among the old guard or the new generation of Sandinistas to replace Ortega. "One major power in the party is Ortega's brother and main adviser, Humberto Ortega. Politically, he is very capable, but his handicap is that he is part of the old guard," Sanchez said.
Humberto Ortega headed the army during the Sandinista regime and for several years under Chamorro, his brother's successor as president.

Similarly, traditional Sandinista commanders such as Tomas Borge or Bayardo Arce carry too much historical baggage to be elected president, Rene Vargas said. He said a new, relatively unknown candidate unsullied by the scandals and problems of the past might emerge to give a new face to the Sandinistas.

Although they lost the election, the Sandinistas captured a hefty bloc of seats in the National Assembly, many mayorships and almost 40 percent support nationwide. Analysts agreed it was too early to write them off as a political force. Since even before they toppled former dictator Anastasio Somoza in the 1979 revolution, the Sandinistas have survived many internal divisions.
